report.summary: An authentication anomaly was detected involving user 'user01' connecting from source IP 203.0.113.80 to host WS-25. The sequence comprised 5 consecutive failed network logon attempts (Event ID 4625, Logon Type 3) between 08:01:25Z and 08:03:45Z, immediately followed by a successful network logon (Event ID 4624) at 08:04:40Z.

findings.title: Multiple Consecutive Failed Logon Attempts
findings.explanation: Five consecutive failed network logon attempts (Logon Type 3, Windows Event ID 4625) occurred within approximately 2.5 minutes from source IP 203.0.113.80 targeted at user 'user01' on host WS-25.

findings.title: Authentication Success Following Failures
findings.explanation: Following the 5 failed logon attempts, a successful network logon (Logon Type 3, Windows Event ID 4624) was recorded from the exact same source IP 203.0.113.80 for 'user01' on WS-25 less than a minute later.

findings.title: Potential Password Guessing Activity
findings.explanation: The pattern of repeated authentication failures against a single target identity followed quickly by a successful logon is characteristic of iterative password guessing attempts.

why_suspicious.reason: Rapid successive authentication failures for an account followed by a sudden success from an external/remote IP (203.0.113.80) matches patterns of brute force or password guessing behavior.

mitre_techniques.name: Password Guessing
mitre_techniques.reason: Repeated network logon failures against user01 followed by a successful logon indicate potential password guessing across standard services generating Event ID 4625/4624.

recommended_actions.action: Investigate subsequent process executions and user activity on WS-25 under account user01 following the successful logon at 08:04:40Z.
recommended_actions.reason: To determine whether unauthorized post-authentication actions or persistence mechanisms were established following the successful logon.

recommended_actions.action: Verify the ownership and legitimacy of source IP 203.0.113.80 and consult with the user regarding their login attempts.
recommended_actions.reason: To rule out legitimate user mistyping of passwords versus unauthorized external access attempts.

recommended_actions.action: Consider credential reset for user01 and examine host WS-25 for any indicators of compromise.
recommended_actions.reason: If the source IP 203.0.113.80 is confirmed unauthorized, the account credentials should be considered compromised.

limitations: Process details, command lines, destination ports, and specific failure sub-status codes (e.g., bad password vs. locked account) were not populated in the event evidence.
No post-logon activity logs are present in the provided evidence to confirm actions taken during the active session.

report.summary: On host WS-75, an instance of Microsoft Word (WINWORD.EXE) spawned a PowerShell process executing a command on behalf of user user04.

timeline.description: WINWORD.EXE (PID 7063) was launched by explorer.exe (PID 6535) with the command line 'WINWORD.EXE <synthetic-document>' for user user04 on host WS-75.
WINWORD.EXE (PID 7063) spawned powershell.exe (PID 51221) with command line 'powershell.exe -Command "<synthetic-office-action>"' for user user04 on host WS-75.

findings.title: Office Process Spawns PowerShell Script Interpreter
findings.explanation: Microsoft Word (WINWORD.EXE, PID 7063) directly created a child process running powershell.exe (PID 51221) with the command line argument '-Command "<synthetic-office-action>"'.

findings.title: Potential Malicious Execution via Office Application
findings.explanation: Execution of script interpreters such as PowerShell directly spawned by Office applications is commonly indicative of macro-based or document-based code execution attempts.

why_suspicious.reason: Word processing applications such as WINWORD.EXE should rarely directly invoke command and script interpreters like powershell.exe under normal business operations.
PowerShell was invoked directly by an Office parent with inline command parameters (-Command), matching common script interpreter abuse techniques.

mitre_techniques.name: PowerShell
mitre_techniques.reason: Adversaries abuse PowerShell commands and scripts for execution, as demonstrated by the invocation of powershell.exe with the -Command parameter from WINWORD.EXE.

mitre_techniques.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
mitre_techniques.reason: Adversaries abuse command and script interpreters such as PowerShell embedded in or spawned from client applications to achieve execution.

recommended_actions.action: Inspect the document file opened by WINWORD.EXE on WS-75 to identify embedded macros, scripts, or external templates.
recommended_actions.reason: To verify if the document contains unauthorized macros or malicious code responsible for triggering the PowerShell process.

recommended_actions.action: Review host process tree and script block logs for PowerShell PID 51221 and subsequent child processes on host WS-75.
recommended_actions.reason: To determine what actions, network connections, or file modifications were attempted by the PowerShell execution.

recommended_actions.action: Examine host and network telemetry for any outbound network connections initiated around 2026-01-18T08:01:34Z from WS-75.
recommended_actions.reason: To detect potential secondary payload downloads or command and control communication.

limitations: The full content of the synthetic document and the exact commands executed inside '<synthetic-office-action>' are masked or not provided in the telemetry.
Network event logs and file modification logs are not present in the provided evidence to determine subsequent activity following PowerShell execution.
